'''Gonzalez:''' {{legend0|#A5B0FF|40–50%}} {{legend0|#7996e2|50–60%}} {{legend0|#6674de|60–70%}} {{legend0|#584cde|70–80%}}
'''Tie:''' {{legend0|#d2b1d9|40–50%}} {{legend0|#ae8bb1|50%}} | title = [[Governor of Massachusetts|Governor]] | before_election = [[Charlie Baker]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Charlie Baker]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsMA}} The '''2018 Massachusetts gubernatorial election''' took place on November 6, 2018, to elect the [[Governor of Massachusetts|governor]] and [[Lieutenant Governor of Massachusetts|lieutenant governor]] of the [[Massachusetts|Commonwealth of Massachusetts]]. [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] Governor [[Charlie Baker]] and Lieutenant Governor [[Karyn Polito]] won election to a second term in office, defeating [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] challengers [[Jay Gonzalez (politician)|Jay Gonzalez]] and [[Quentin Palfrey]], respectively. Candidates were selected in the [[Partisan primary|primary election]] held on September 4, 2018. This was one of eight Republican-held governorships up for election in a state that [[Hillary Clinton]] won in the [[2016 United States presidential election in Massachusetts|2016 presidential election]]. Despite Massachusetts's Democratic lean at the presidential level, Charlie Baker retained high approval ratings and was expected to safely win re-election. Shortly after polls closed at 8 p.m. local time, the [[Associated Press]] declared the race in favor of incumbents Baker and Polito.{{cite news |url=https://www.boston.com/news/politics/2018/11/06/massachusetts-election-results-2018/ |title=Here's an updating list of the 2018 Massachusetts election winners |first=Christopher |last=Gavin |website=[[Boston.com]] |date=November 6, 2018 |access-date=November 6, 2018}} Shortly after 9 p.m. location time, Gonzalez conceded the election.{{cite tweet |user=MattPStout |number=1059993577026211840 |title=@jay4ma has conceded to @CharlieBakerMA |date=November 6, 2018 |access-date=November 6, 2018}} Baker was re-elected with the highest vote total in the history of Massachusetts gubernatorial elections and by the widest margin since [[Bill Weld]] was re-elected governor in [[1994 Massachusetts gubernatorial election|1994]]. He won many of the Commonwealth's most populated cities, including [[Worcester, Massachusetts|Worcester]], [[New Bedford]], and [[Springfield, Massachusetts|Springfield]].{{cite news |url=https://whdh.com/news/bakers-big-win-a-gop-anomaly-in-heavily-democratic-state/ |work=[[WHDH-TV]] |title=Baker's big win a GOP anomaly in heavily-Democratic state |date=November 7, 2018 |access-date=December 30, 2020}} Baker almost won [[Boston]], losing it by only around 3,000 votes, an extraordinary showing for a statewide Republican candidate in a major city. Baker also carried every county in the state.{{cite news |url=https://www.masslive.com/news/boston/2018/11/2018_massachusetts_election_re.html |work=MassLive |title=2018 Massachusetts Election: Republican Gov. Charlie Baker almost won Democrat-dominated Boston |date=November 7, 2018 |access-date=December 30, 2020}} {{As of|2026}}, this is the most recent election in which a Republican was elected to a statewide office in Massachusetts. {{TOC limit|3}} ==Background== Charlie Baker was elected in 2014 by a slim margin over then-Attorney General [[Martha Coakley]]; however, he was consistently rated as one of the most popular governors in the country.{{cite web|url=https://boston.cbslocal.com/2018/04/12/charlie-baker-poll-morning-consult-most-popular/|title=Poll: Charlie Baker Is Once Again America's Most Popular Governor|date=April 12, 2018 |publisher=WBZ}} Some Democrats, including Congressman [[Michael Capuano|Mike Capuano]] and Speaker of the House [[Robert DeLeo (politician)|Bob DeLeo]] publicly, speculated that they might vote for Baker over the eventual Democratic nominee.{{cite web|url=http://www.bostonherald.com/news/us_politics/2017/08/mike_capuano_may_dodge_party_lines_in_gubernatorial_vote|title=Mike Capuano may dodge party lines in gubernatorial vote|date=23 August 2017 |publisher=Boston Herald}} Speculated candidates such as Attorney General [[Maura Healey]], Congressman [[Joe Kennedy III|Joe Kennedy]], former state senator [[Dan Wolf]], and [[Boston, Massachusetts|Boston]] Mayor [[Marty Walsh]] all declined to be candidates, leaving no prominent Democrats to challenge Baker, which was seen as a necessary prerequisite to mount a formidable challenge to him. Because Evan Falchuk received more than 3% of the vote in the [[Massachusetts gubernatorial election, 2014|2014 gubernatorial election]], the [[United Independent Party]] gained official status.{{cite news|url=http://news.wgbh.org/post/united-independent-party-gains-official-status|title=United Independent Party Gains Official Status|last=Emmanouilidou|first=Lydia|date=November 6, 2014|work=[[WGBH (FM)]]|access-date=7 November 2014|archive-date=September 20, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160920094359/http://news.wgbh.org/post/united-independent-party-gains-official-status|url-status=dead}} Falchuck had stated that he would "certainly" run for office in 2018.{{cite news|last=Morrison|first=Sara|title=The United Independent Party Is Official, and Evan Falchuk's Work Has Just Begun|newspaper=Boston.com|date=November 5, 2014|url=http://www.huffingtonpost.com/2014/11/17/future-democratic-candidates_n_6152346.html}} In 2016, however, the UIP lost its official party status after it failed to register 1% of Massachusetts voters as members.{{cite news|url=https://www.politico.com/states/massachusetts/story/2016/10/united-independent-party-loses-state-party-designation-106905|title=United Independent Party loses state party designation|last=Dezenski|first=Lauren|date=October 31, 2016|work=[[Politico]]|access-date=23 January 2017}} Falchuk later left the UIP and registered as a Democrat in early 2017.{{cite web|url=https://www.bostonglobe.com/metro/2017/02/12/switch/b84oZEjZyFyGSnn5OHl5jO/story.html#comments|title=Evan Falchuk, former gubernatorial candidate, switches from his independent party to Democratic - The Boston Globe|website=[[The Boston Globe]] |access-date=22 May 2018}}{{cite web|url=https://www.politico.com/states/massachusetts/story/2016/10/united-independent-party-loses-state-party-designation-106905|title=United Independent Party loses state party designation|website=[[Politico]] |date=October 31, 2016 |access-date=22 May 2018}} ==Republican primary== There was some concern amongst the Republican Party that Baker was too moderate, and there were talks of challenging him with a more conservative opponent in the primaries. GOP state committeeman Robert Cappucci told the ''[[Boston Herald]]'' that if Baker "shuns conservatives [...] there will be 100 percent an effort to try to find a conservative, viable candidate to challenge him in 2018 for governor". David Kopacz, the president of the Massachusetts Republican Assembly, also stated that Baker might face a conservative challenger in 2018.{{cite news|last1=Stout|first1=Matt|last2=Cassidy|first2=Chris|title=Waiting for Mr. Right: Conservative wing of GOP warns Charlie Baker|newspaper=Boston Herald|date=November 13, 2014}} Following his 2016 election, [[Barnstable County, Massachusetts|Barnstable County]] Commissioner Ron Beaty, who once was tried and convicted for threatening the life of President [[George H. W. Bush]],{{cite news|url=http://www.barnstablepatriot.com/home2/index.php/option=com_content/task=view/id=37289/Itemid=30|last=Hoffenburg|first=Noah|title=Ronald Beaty, Jr.|newspaper=Barnstable Patriot|date=August 29, 2014}} had been making local and state headlines. He proposed a "shark mitigation strategy" to combat the growing presence of sharks near [[Cape Cod]] beaches by baiting and shooting them, which was rejected for consideration by the commission chairman. He also mulled a primary run against his state representative, [[Randy Hunt (politician)|Randy Hunt]], after Hunt parked in his Barnstable County Courthouse parking spot. In September 2017 he announced he was in the process of changing the purpose of his campaign committee from a county to a statewide office. He cited the governor's criticisms of President [[Donald Trump]] and his willingness to work with Democrats as his inspiration to run. On December 8, 2017, Scott Lively announced his campaign.{{cite web | url=https://sites.google.com/view/thirdpartywatch/secret/scott-lively-former-independent-candidate-is-running-for-the-republican?authuser=2 | title=Scott Lively, Former Independent Candidate, Is Running For The Republican Nomination | publisher=Third Party Watch | date=December 8, 2017}} On December 13, 2017, Beaty stated he was no longer considering a run against Baker.{{cite web|url=http://www.capecodtoday.com/article/2017/12/13/236270-Beaty-Ends-Exploratory-Project-Gov-Run|title=Beaty Ends Exploratory Project on Gov. Run - CapeCodToday.com|website=www.capecodtoday.com|access-date=22 May 2018|archive-date=13 December 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171213203337/http://capecodtoday.com/article/2017/12/13/236270-Beaty-Ends-Exploratory-Project-Gov-Run|url-status=dead}} [[Scott Lively]], an evangelical pastor, challenged Baker and received more than the 15% of delegate votes necessary at the state convention to qualify for ballot access. Baker won the endorsement of the party by an overwhelming margin.{{cite web|url=https://worcestermag.com/2018/04/28/baker-earns-states-gop-endorsement-for-governor-scott-lively-forces-primary/59244|title=Baker earns states GOP endorsement for governor; Scott Lively forces primary - Worcester Mag|first=Walter Jr.|last=Bird|date=28 April 2018|access-date=22 May 2018}}{{Dead link|date=April 2023 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} Baker ultimately won the nomination, but not without Lively securing 36 percent of the primary vote, leading to speculation that Baker's more moderate disposition and opposition to President Trump might have damaged his general election chances with Republican base voters.{{cite web | url=https://commonwealthmagazine.org/politics/the-bay-state-trump-bump-2/ | title=The Bay State Trump bump | publisher=Commonwealth Magazine | date=September 5, 2018 | access-date=September 5, 2018 | archive-date=September 5, 2018 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180905214927/https://commonwealthmagazine.org/politics/the-bay-state-trump-bump-2/ | url-status=dead }} ===Governor=== ====Candidates==== =====Declared===== * [[Charlie Baker]], incumbent governor{{cite news|url=https://www.boston.com/news/politics/2017/11/28/charlie-baker-confirms-run-for-2nd-term-as-massachusetts-governor/|title=Charlie Baker confirms run for 2nd term as Massachusetts governor|work=[[The Boston Globe]]|last=Salsberg|first=Bob|date=November 28, 2017|access-date=November 28, 2017}} * [[Scott Lively]], pastor and independent candidate for governor in [[Massachusetts gubernatorial election, 2014|2014]]{{cite news|url=http://www.masslive.com/politics/index.ssf/2017/12/anti-lgbt_springfield_pastor_s.html|title=Anti-LGBT Springfield pastor Scott Lively to challenge Gov. He identified Attorney General [[Maura Healey]] as being "the first name on many Democratic lists".{{cite news|last=Miller|first=Joshua|title=Mass. Democrats are on to 2018|newspaper=The Boston Globe|date=November 13, 2014|url=https://www.bostonglobe.com/metro/2014/11/13/and-now/aR88GX2jjZJCo7qBbek12I/story.html}} Samantha Lachman of ''[[The Huffington Post]]'' also identified Healey as a potential candidate for governor in 2018 or in a future [[United States Senate]] race.{{cite news|last=Lachman|first=Samantha|title=These Democrats Could Be The Party's Ticket To A Comeback|newspaper=Huffington Post|date=November 17, 2014|url=http://www.huffingtonpost.com/2014/11/17/future-democratic-candidates_n_6152346.html}} As of July 2017, the declared candidates were relatively unknown to the state's voters.{{Cite news|url=http://www.masslive.com/news/index.ssf/2017/06/this_massachusetts_democrat_co.html|title=This Massachusetts Democrat comes closest to beating Gov. Charlie Baker in 2018, WBUR/MassINC poll says|work=masslive.com|access-date=2017-07-22|language=en-US}} Their identification by Democratic voters was bolstered by addressing the 2017 state Democratic Convention, which saw its largest attendance in years, of around 3,000 delegates.{{Cite news|url=http://www.masslive.com/politics/index.ssf/2017/06/who_can_beat_gov_charlie_baker.html|title=Who can beat Gov. Charlie Baker?: Candidates make their cases at the Massachusetts Democratic Convention in Worcester|work=masslive.com|access-date=2017-07-22|language=en-US}} On April 26, 2018, [[Setti Warren]] announced via Facebook that he was withdrawing from the race due to financial concerns. He stated he would not endorse either of his former opponents until the nomination was won.{{cite web|last1=Phillips|first1=Frank|title=Setti Warren ends campaign for governor|url=https://www.bostonglobe.com/metro/2018/04/26/setti-warren-end-campaign-for-governor/vQqKoCGuCBYBuFzReqG2EO/story.html|website=The Boston Globe|access-date=26 April 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180426124903/http://www.bostonglobe.com/metro/2018/04/26/setti-warren-end-campaign-for-governor/vQqKoCGuCBYBuFzReqG2EO/story.html|archive-date=26 April 2018|url-status=dead}} At the Massachusetts Democratic Convention in June, party delegates endorsed Gonzalez and Palfrey, but Bob Massie and Jimmy Tingle also surpassed the 15% threshold for ballot access by comfortable margins.{{Cite web|url=https://www.wbur.org/news/2018/06/02/mass-democrats-endorse-gonzalez-palfrey-zakim|title=Mass. Democrats Endorse Gonzalez, Palfrey And Zakim At Convention|website=www.wbur.org|date=June 3, 2018 }} A poll from late June conducted by WBUR and MassInc. indicated that the contest for the Democratic nomination in the gubernatorial race was a toss-up, with Massie and Gonzalez being separated by a percentage smaller than the margin of error. 2018 Maryland gubernatorial election.text:

'''Tie:''' {{legend0|#d2b1d9|40–50%}} {{legend0|#ae8bb1|50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No data}} | title = [[Governor of Maryland|Governor]] | before_election = [[Larry Hogan]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Larry Hogan]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) }} {{Elections in Maryland sidebar}} The '''2018 Maryland gubernatorial election''' was held on November 6, 2018. The date included the election of the [[Governor of Maryland|governor]], [[Lieutenant Governor of Maryland|lieutenant governor]], and all members of the [[Maryland General Assembly]]. Popular incumbent Governor [[Larry Hogan]] and Lieutenant Governor [[Boyd Rutherford]], both [[Maryland Republican Party|Republicans]], were elected to a second term in a landslide against Democrat [[Ben Jealous]], the former [[NAACP]] CEO, and his running mate [[Susan Turnbull]]. This was one of eight Republican-held governorships up for election in a state carried by [[Hillary Clinton]] in the [[2016 United States presidential election|2016 presidential election]]. Hogan became the second Republican governor of Maryland to win re-election, and the first since [[Theodore McKeldin]] in [[1954 Maryland gubernatorial election|1954]].{{cite news |url=https://www.wbaltv.com/article/hogan-becomes-first-gop-governor-to-win-second-term-in-maryland-since-1954/24510818 |title=Gov. Larry Hogan makes history with re-election in Maryland |first1=Greg |last1=Ng |publisher=[[WBAL-TV]] |date=November 6, 2018 |first2=Kate |last2=Amara |access-date=November 7, 2018}} He also became the first Republican to win over 55% of the vote in a statewide election in Maryland since U.S. Senator [[Charles Mathias]] in [[1980 United States Senate election in Maryland|1980]]. This was the first election since 1974 in which Maryland simultaneously elected a gubernatorial nominee and a U.S. Senate nominee of opposite parties. This was the first and only Maryland gubernatorial election in which both major party candidates received over one million votes. As of 2025, this is the last time that a Republican won a statewide election in Maryland. ==Background== At the presidential level, [[Maryland]] is a staunchly Democratic state due to the large number of Democratic voters in the [[Washington metropolitan area]] and [[Baltimore]] City. Maryland had not seen a Republican presidential candidate win its votes since 1988, and the state had not been within 15% since [[2004 United States presidential election in Maryland|2004]]; [[Hillary Clinton]] won the state by 26 points over [[Donald Trump]] (60% to 34%) in 2016, [[Barack Obama]] defeated [[Mitt Romney]] by 26 points in 2012 (62% to 36%), and Obama defeated [[John McCain]] by 25 points in 2008 (62% to 37%). Hogan was elected governor in [[2014 Maryland gubernatorial election|2014]], defeating then-lieutenant governor [[Anthony Brown (Maryland politician)|Anthony Brown]] by a margin of 51% to 47%; the result was considered one of the biggest election upsets that year.{{Cite web |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/md-politics/republican-larry-hogan-wins-md-governors-race-in-stunning-upset/2014/11/05/9eb8bf46-60ac-11e4-8b9e-2ccdac31a031_story.html |title=Republican Larry Hogan wins Md. governor's race in stunning upset |access-date=2018-08-10 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180803154213/https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/md-politics/republican-larry-hogan-wins-md-governors-race-in-stunning-upset/2014/11/05/9eb8bf46-60ac-11e4-8b9e-2ccdac31a031_story.html |archive-date=2018-08-03 |url-status=live |date=November 5, 2014 |newspaper=The Washington Post |first1=John |last1=Wagner |first2=Jenna |last2=Johnson }} Prior to Hogan's victory, [[Bob Ehrlich]], elected in [[2002 Maryland gubernatorial election|2002]], had been the only Republican elected as Governor of Maryland since [[Spiro Agnew]]. However, Ehrlich was defeated for reelection in [[2006 Maryland gubernatorial election|2006]] by [[Martin O'Malley]] and defeated again in [[2010 Maryland gubernatorial election|2010]], when he faced O'Malley in a rematch. In April 2018, Hogan had a 68% approval rating, the second-highest approval of any governor in the country, only behind Governor [[Charlie Baker]] of Massachusetts, who had a 71% approval rating.{{cite news|url=http://www.dbknews.com/2018/04/19/larry-hogan-approval-rating-maryland-governor-election/|title=Larry Hogan is the second-most popular governor in the US, a poll shows|newspaper=The Diamondback|access-date=October 31, 2018|first=Brooks|last=DuBose|archive-date=November 10, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181110115800/http://www.dbknews.com/2018/04/19/larry-hogan-approval-rating-maryland-governor-election/|url-status=dead}} Despite the state's Democratic leaning, Hogan had a high approval rating among all partisan groups (65% approval from Democrats, 64% of Independents, and 81% of Republicans).{{cite news |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/md-politics/poll-hogans-approval-ratings-sky-high-democrats-stronger-among-women-millenials/2018/04/23/ae79f614-4705-11e8-8b5a-3b1697adcc2a_story.html |title=Poll: Hogan's approval ratings sky-high; Mills|Janet Mills]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsME}} The '''2018 Maine gubernatorial election''' took place on November 6, 2018, to elect the [[governor of Maine]]. It occurred along with elections for the [[United States Senate election in Maine, 2018|U.S. Senate]], [[United States House of Representatives elections in Maine, 2018|U.S. House]], and other state and local elections. Incumbent [[Maine Republican Party|Republican]] Governor [[Paul LePage]] was term-limited and could not seek a third consecutive term. He later unsuccessfully sought a third term in [[2022 Maine gubernatorial election|2022]].{{Cite web |last=WMTW |date=2022-11-09 |title=Former Gov. LePage concedes, cites 'grave' concerns over inflation for Maine |url=https://www.wabi.tv/2022/11/09/former-gov-lepage-concedes-cites-grave-concerns-over-inflation-maine/ |access-date=2023-09-18 |website=www.wabi.tv |language=en}} This was one of eight Republican-held governorships up for election in a state carried by [[Hillary Clinton]] in the [[2016 United States presidential election|2016 presidential election]]. The primaries for this election were the first in Maine to be conducted with [[Instant-runoff voting|ranked choice voting]] (RCV), as opposed to a simple plurality, after voters passed [[Maine Question 5, 2016|a citizen referendum]] approving the change in 2016.{{cite news|title=Maine became the first state in the country Tuesday to pass ranked choice voting|url=https://www.boston.com/news/politics/2016/11/10/maine-became-the-first-state-in-the-country-to-pass-ranked-choice-voting/|access-date=November 17, 2016|newspaper=Boston Globe|date=November 10, 2016|archive-date=November 16, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161116075525/https://www.boston.com/news/politics/2016/11/10/maine-became-the-first-state-in-the-country-to-pass-ranked-choice-voting|url-status=live}} An [[advisory opinion]] by the [[Maine Supreme Judicial Court]] held that RCV would be unconstitutional for general elections for governor and the state legislature. This led state legislators to vote to delay its implementation pending approval of a state constitutional amendment.{{cite news|title=Maine Supreme Judicial Court rules ranked-choice voting unconstitutional|url=http://bangordailynews.com/2017/05/23/politics/maine-supreme-judicial-court-rules-ranked-choice-voting-unconstitutional/|access-date=May 23, 2016|newspaper=Bangor Daily News|date=May 23, 2016|archive-date=May 23, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170523181148/https://bangordailynews.com/2017/05/23/politics/maine-supreme-judicial-court-rules-ranked-choice-voting-unconstitutional/|url-status=live}}{{cite web|url=http://www.wcsh6.com/news/politics/loose-ends-bring-legislature-back-for-special-session/485282422|title=Ranked choice voting delayed until 2021|last=TEGNA}}{{Dead link|date=June 2022 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} Backers of a "people's veto" turned in enough signatures to suspend this law until a [[Maine Question 1, June 2018|June referendum vote]], which restored RCV for future primary and congressional elections.{{cite news|title=Voters will decide in June whether Maine keeps its ranked-choice voting law|url=https://www.pressherald.com/2018/03/05/voters-in-june-will-decide-if-maine-keeps-its-ranked-choice-voting-law/|access-date=March 16, 2018|newspaper=Portland Press Herald|date=March 5, 2018|archive-date=March 16, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180316152425/https://www.pressherald.com/2018/03/05/voters-in-june-will-decide-if-maine-keeps-its-ranked-choice-voting-law/|url-status=live}} Governor [[Paul LePage]] threatened not to certify the results of the primary elections, saying he would "leave it up to the courts to decide."{{cite news |last=Nilsen |first=Ella |publisher=Vox |title=Maine's governor is threatening not to certify the results of Tuesday's primary |access-date=June 13, 2018 |url=https://www.vox.com/2018/6/12/17453676/paul-lepage-maine-governor-threatening-not-to-certify-tuesday-primary-results-2018-midterms |archive-date=June 13, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180613012711/https://www.vox.com/2018/6/12/17453676/paul-lepage-maine-governor-threatening-not-to-certify-tuesday-primary-results-2018-midterms |url-status=live }} He also called the use of ranked-choice voting the "most horrific thing in the world."{{cite news |last=Levine |first=Sam |publisher=Huffington Post |title=Maine Gov. Paul LePage 'Probably' Won't Certify Primary Election Results |access-date=June 13, 2018 |url=https://www.huffingtonpost.com/entry/paul-lepage-ranked-choice-voting_us_5b203bf1e4b09d7a3d781600 |archive-date=June 13, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180613012659/https://www.huffingtonpost.com/entry/paul-lepage-ranked-choice-voting_us_5b203bf1e4b09d7a3d781600 |url-status=live }} Secretary of State [[Matthew Dunlap]] said the results would be binding regardless of whether LePage certified them.{{Cite news|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2018/06/13/republican-sanford-loses-in-south-carolina-after-trump-urges-his-ouster.html|title=Republican Sanford loses in South Carolina after Trump urges his ouster|work=[[CNBC]]|quote=Maine Secretary of State Matt Dunlap said the election results would be binding anyway, the Portland Press Herald said.|access-date=July 8, 2018|archive-date=July 8, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180708075402/https://www.cnbc.com/2018/06/13/republican-sanford-loses-in-south-carolina-after-trump-urges-his-ouster.html|url-status=live}} The Republican nominee was businessman and [[Maine gubernatorial election, 2010|2010 independent candidate]] for governor Shawn Moody. The [[Maine Democratic Party|Democratic]] candidate was [[Maine Attorney General|Attorney General]] [[Janet T. Mills|Janet Mills]]. [[Maine State Treasurer|State Treasurer]] [[Terry Hayes (politician)|Terry Hayes]] and businessman Alan Caron had qualified for the ballot as independents, though Caron dropped out on October 29 and endorsed Mills. Former state senator and former mayor of [[Lewiston, Maine|Lewiston]] and [[Auburn, Maine|Auburn]] John Jenkins and perennial candidate Kenneth Capron ran write-in campaigns. Mills defeated Moody and Hayes with a majority to become the first female governor of Maine. This was the first election since [[2006 Maine gubernatorial election|2006]] that Maine elected a Democratic governor. Mills was also the first gubernatorial candidate to win at least 50% of the vote since [[Angus King]] in [[Maine gubernatorial election, 1998|1998]], and the first non-incumbent to do so since [[Kenneth M. Curtis]] in [[Maine gubernatorial election, 1966|1966]]. Mills received more votes for governor than any other candidate in Maine history, becoming the first Maine gubernatorial candidate to earn 300,000 votes. This was the first gubernatorial election since [[1982 Maine gubernatorial election|1982]] that a Democrat would win a majority of the popular vote.{{Cite web|url=https://uselectionatlas.org/RESULTS/state.php?fips=23&year=1982&off=5&elect=0|title=1982 Gubernatorial General Election Results - Maine|accessdate=April 4, 2023}} ==Background== Incumbent Republican [[Paul LePage]] was term-limited, having been elected twice consecutively in [[Maine gubernatorial election, 2010|2010]] and [[Maine gubernatorial election, 2014|2014]]. LePage did not win a majority of the vote either time (receiving 37.6% in a crowded four-way race in 2010 and 48.2% in a three-way race in 2014), with Democrats accusing independent candidate [[Eliot Cutler]] of splitting the anti-LePage vote in both instances, though Cutler finished closer to LePage than Democratic candidate [[Libby Mitchell]] in the 2010 election.{{cite web|url=http://www.msnbc.com/rachel-maddow-show/republican-governors-association-exploits-its-pawn-maine|title=Republican Governors Association exploits its pawn in Maine|publisher=MSNBC|author=Steve Benen |author-link=Steve Benen|date=October 28, 2014|access-date=January 20, 2018|archive-date=January 21, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180121184314/http://www.msnbc.com/rachel-maddow-show/republican-governors-association-exploits-its-pawn-maine|url-status=live}} Maine's history of governors elected without majorities, including LePage, was one impetus for the [[Maine Question 5, 2016|citizen's referendum]] to implement [[Instant-runoff voting|ranked choice voting]].{{cite web|url=http://bangordailynews.com/2014/10/27/politics/elections/maine-lawmakers-seek-to-end-strategic-voting-spoilers-with-petition-for-ranked-choice-voting/?ref=relatedBox|title=Maine lawmakers seek to end strategic voting, 'spoilers' with petition for ranked-choice voting|publisher=Bangor Daily News|date=October 27, 2015|access-date=January 20, 2018|archive-date=March 23, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160323104140/http://bangordailynews.com/2014/10/27/politics/elections/maine-lawmakers-seek-to-end-strategic-voting-spoilers-with-petition-for-ranked-choice-voting/?ref=relatedBox|url-status=live}}{{cite web|url=http://www.rcvmaine.com/whats_the_problem_with_our_current_voting_system|title=What's the problem with our current voting system?|publisher=The Committee for Ranked Choice Voting|access-date=January 29, 2018|archive-date=January 30, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180130091512/http://www.rcvmaine.com/whats_the_problem_with_our_current_voting_system|url-status=usurped}} Indeed, the last time a gubernatorial candidate received a majority of the vote was in [[Maine gubernatorial election, 1998|1998]], when incumbent governor (and current United States Senator) [[Angus King]], an independent, won reelection with 58.6% of the vote. The last time a non-incumbent candidate received more than 50% of the vote was the [[Maine gubernatorial election, 1966|1966 gubernatorial election]], which Democrat [[Kenneth M. Curtis]] won over incumbent Republican [[John H. Reed]] with 53.1% of the vote. Though ranked-choice voting was approved by voters in a [[Maine Question 5, 2016|2016 referendum]], the [[Maine Legislature]] voted to delay and potentially repeal RCV for all elections after an [[advisory opinion]] by the [[Maine Supreme Judicial Court]] ruled it unconstitutional for general elections for state offices. RCV supporters succeeded in a people's veto effort to prevent the delay, which suspends it until a June 2018 referendum vote.{{cite web|url=https://www.pressherald.com/2018/02/02/ranked-choice-voters-submit-signatures-for-peoples-veto-ballot-initiative/|title=Ranked-choice voters submit signatures for 'people's veto' ballot initiative|date=February 2, 2018|access-date=February 3, 2018|archive-date=February 3, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180203181522/https://www.pressherald.com/2018/02/02/ranked-choice-voters-submit-signatures-for-peoples-veto-ballot-initiative/|url-status=live}} RCV supporters were victorious in the June referendum, and ranked-choice voting will remain in place for state and federal primaries and federal general elections.{{cite web|url=https://www.theatlantic.com/politics/archive/2018/06/maine-lepage-ranked-choice-voting/562871/|title=Maine Voters Overrule Their Leaders|first=Russell|last=Berman|work=[[The Atlantic]]|date=June 15, 2018|access-date=June 21, 2018|archive-date=June 22, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180622005052/https://www.theatlantic.com/politics/archive/2018/06/maine-lepage-ranked-choice-voting/562871/|url-status=live}} ==Republican primary== Speculation that U.S. Senator [[Susan Collins]] was considering running for governor arose during the 2015 [[Maine Legislature|Maine Legislative]] session when Representative [[Matt Moonen]] (D-Portland) introduced a bill to strip the governor (LePage at the time) of the power to appoint replacement U.S. Senators in the event of a vacancy and to instead have a special primary and general election. Moonen denied that he was motivated by Collins's possible candidacy, saying he was interested only in counterbalancing Republican-sponsored bills to change how the [[Maine Attorney General]] and [[Maine Secretary of State]] are chosen. Moonen said Collins had told him speculation about her running for governor was "silly."{{cite news|title=Lawmaker says his bill isn't about Susan Collins running for governor|url=http://bangordailynews.com/2015/03/30/politics/state-house/lawmaker-says-his-bill-isnt-about-susan-collins-running-for-governor/|access-date=March 31, 2015|newspaper=Bangor Daily News|date=March 30, 2014|archive-date=August 15, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150815064441/http://bangordailynews.com/2015/03/30/politics/state-house/lawmaker-says-his-bill-isnt-about-susan-collins-running-for-governor/|url-status=live}} Collins, who was the [[Maine gubernatorial election, 1994|1994 Republican nominee for Governor]], told [[MPBN]] News on January 4, 2016, that though she was "baffled" by the rumors about her being interested in running for governor, many had encouraged her to run, and she would not rule it out.{{cite news|title=Collins Says She Is Baffled By Rumor She Is Running For Governor|url=http://news.mpbn.net/post/collins-says-she-baffled-rumor-she-running-governor|access-date=January 4, 2016|newspaper=MPBN News|date=January 4, 2016|archive-date=January 6, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160106045544/http://news.mpbn.net/post/collins-says-she-baffled-rumor-she-running-governor|url-status=live}} In October 2017, Collins said she would not run for governor in 2018.Cook, Janet. "[https://www.wsj.com/articles/susan-collins-to-remain-in-u-s-senate-1507900816?mod=e2tw Susan Collins to Remain in U.S. Senate] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171013224934/https://www.wsj.com/articles/susan-collins-to-remain-in-u-s-senate-1507900816?mod=e2tw |date=October 13, 2017}}". ''The Wall Street Journal''. October 13, 2017. No Republican candidate ruled out challenging the results of a ranked-choice primary in court. [[Mary Mayhew]] called for the immediate repeal of RCV, calling it a "scam" and "probably illegal".{{cite news|title=Candidates for Blaine House signal they might challenge outcome of a ranked-choice vote|url=https://www.pressherald.com/2018/04/07/candidates-for-maine-governor-signal-they-might-challenge-outcome-of-ranked-choice-vote/|access-date=April 7, 2018|newspaper=Portland Press Herald|date=April 7, 2018|archive-date=April 7, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180407105028/https://www.pressherald.com/2018/04/07/candidates-for-maine-governor-signal-they-might-challenge-outcome-of-ranked-choice-vote/|url-status=live}} The [[Maine Republican Party]] filed a federal lawsuit in U.S. District Court in [[Bangor, Maine|Bangor]] on May 4, 2018, seeking to bar the use of RCV for its own primary on the grounds that requiring the party to use it violates its [[First Amendment to the United States Constitution|First Amendment]] rights to choose its nominee as it sees fit.{{Cite news |url=http://mainepublic.org/post/gop-files-suit-block-ranked-choice-voting |title=GOP Files Suit To Block Ranked-Choice Voting |last=Leary |first=Mal |date=May 4, 2018 |publisher=[[MPBN]] |access-date=May 7, 2018 |archive-date=May 7, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180507221443/http://mainepublic.org/post/gop-files-suit-block-ranked-choice-voting |url-status=live}} U.S. Woodbury]], former state senator == General election == After the primaries, most prediction models had the race as a tossup, noting Paul LePage's two victories and [[Hillary Clinton]]'s narrow margin of victory in the state in the [[2016 United States presidential election|2016 presidential election]]. Others considered it to be a pick-up opportunity for the Democrats.{{Cite news |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2018/10/10/governors-seats-most-likely-flip-parties-november/?noredirect=on |title=The 10 governor's seats most likely to flip parties in November |last=Phillips |first=Amber |date=October 10, 2018 |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |access-date=October 13, 2018 |archive-date=November 25, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181125052217/https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2018/10/10/governors-seats-most-likely-flip-parties-november/?noredirect=on |url-status=live }} Both Moody and Mills received the backing of outside money, with one PAC spending in excess of $1 million on television advertising in the state to support Mills's candidacy.{{Cite news |url=https://www.pressherald.com/2018/09/17/democratic-pac-tops-1-million-in-spending-in-governors-race/ |title=Democratic PAC tops $1 million in spending in Maine governor's race |last=Gallagher |first=Noel K. |date=September 17, 2018 |work=[[The Portland Press Herald]] |access-date=October 13, 2018 |archive-date=October 13, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181013093457/https://www.pressherald.com/2018/09/17/democratic-pac-tops-1-million-in-spending-in-governors-race/ |url-status=live }} On October 12, [[Jonathan Martin (journalist)|Jonathan Martin]] of ''[[The New York Times]]'' published an article detailing a sex discrimination complaint filed against Moody and his business in 2006, which Moody settled for $20,000, resulting in the complaint being withdrawn. The complaint alleged that Moody went to the residence of a female employee and fired her for having a child just days after delivering the child via an emergency [[caesarean section]].{{Cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/10/12/us/politics/shawn-moody-maine-discrimination.html |title=He Settled a Sex Discrimination Complaint. Now He Wants to Lead Maine. |last=Martin |first=Jonathan |date=October 12, 2018 |work=[[The New York Times]] |access-date=October 13, 2018 |archive-date=October 12, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181012204634/https://www.nytimes.com/2018/10/12/us/politics/shawn-moody-maine-discrimination.html |url-status=live }} Moody denied the allegation through a spokesperson and later on Twitter.{{Cite news |url=https://www.wmtw.com/article/moody-responds-to-sex-discrimination-allegation-printed-in-new-york-times/23734297 |title=Moody responds to sex discrimination allegation printed in New York Times |last=Merrill |first=Paul |date=October 12, 2018 |work=[[WMTW (TV)|WMTW-TV]] |access-date=October 13, 2018 |archive-date=October 12, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181012154948/https://www.wmtw.com/article/moody-responds-to-sex-discrimination-allegation-printed-in-new-york-times/23734297 |url-status=live}} Though the first poll of the race saw Mills and Moody tied for first place with Hayes and Caron lagging behind, by the end of October, four different polls were released, each showing Mills with an eight-point lead over Moody. ''[[FiveThirtyEight]]'' declared the race "Likely D" when its gubernatorial projections were released in October, though other prediction models maintained the race as a tossup. On October 29, in a press conference at the main branch of the [[Portland Public Library]], Caron dropped out of the race and endorsed Mills. His name remained on the ballot, but any votes cast for him were regarded as blank.{{Cite news|url=https://bangordailynews.com/2018/10/29/politics/independent-alan-caron-quits-maine-governors-race/|title=Independent Alan Caron quits Maine governor's race|last=Shepherd|first=Michael|date=October 29, 2018|work=[[Bangor Daily News]]|access-date=October 29, 2018|archive-date=October 29, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181029232717/https://bangordailynews.com/2018/10/29/politics/independent-alan-caron-quits-maine-governors-race/|url-status=live}} Shortly before 10 pm on election night, Hayes conceded the race.{{Cite web |url=http://www.mainepublic.org/post/live-updates-democrat-janet-mills-becomes-maines-next-governor#stream/0 |title=Live Updates: Democrat Janet Mills Becomes Maine's Next Governor |date=November 6, 2018 |website=MainePublic.org |access-date=November 7, 2018 |archive-date=October 7, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211007114641/https://www.mainepublic.org/politics/2018-11-06/election-night-2018-live-blog#stream/0 |url-status=live}} At 12:15 am on November 7, Moody conceded the race to Mills, and shortly thereafter Mills declared victory at Democratic headquarters in Portland. Mills became the first Maine gubernatorial candidate to receive more than 300,000 votes in a single election. Mills also became the first Maine gubernatorial candidate to win a majority of the vote since Angus King won nearly 59% of the vote in his re-election bid in [[Maine gubernatorial election, 1998|1998]], and became the first candidate to win a majority of the popular vote for a first term since [[Kenneth M. Curtis]] defeated incumbent governor [[John H. Reed]] in [[Maine gubernatorial election, 1966|1966]], though Curtis and Reed were the only candidates in that race. 2018 Michigan gubernatorial election.text:

'''Tie''': {{legend0|#d2b1d9|40–50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No data}} | title = [[Governor of Michigan|Governor]] | before_election = [[Rick Snyder]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Gretchen Whitmer]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsMI}} The '''2018 Michigan gubernatorial election''' took place on November 6, 2018, to elect the next [[governor of Michigan]], concurrently with the [[2018 United States Senate election in Michigan|election]] of Michigan's [[Classes of United States senators|Class I U.S. Senate seat]], as well as [[2018 United States Senate elections|other elections]] to the United States Senate in other states, [[2018 United States House of Representatives elections|elections]] to the [[United States House of Representatives]], and various [[2018 United States elections#State elections|state]] and [[2018 United States elections#Local elections|local elections]]. Incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] Governor [[Rick Snyder]] and [[Lieutenant Governor of Michigan|Lieutenant Governor]] [[Brian Calley]] were term-limited and were unable to seek a third term in office.{{cite web |url=http://www.freep.com/story/news/local/michigan/2015/02/23/schuette-raising-campaign-money/23876929/ |title=Fund-raiser fuels speculation Schuette eying run for governor |work=[[Detroit Free Press]] |first=Paul |last=Egan |date=February 23, 2015 |access-date=May 28, 2015}} The filing deadline was April 24, 2018. The [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]], [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] and [[Libertarian Party (United States)|Libertarian parties]] chose their nominees in a partisan primary on August 7, 2018.{{cite web |url=http://www.michigan.gov/documents/sos/2018_Dates_600221_7.pdf |title=MICHIGAN ELECTION DATES |work=Michigan Department of State |author=Ruth Johnson, Secretary of State}} 2018 was the first year the Libertarian Party held a gubernatorial primary alongside the two other major parties in the state of Michigan.{{Cite news|url=https://www.detroitnews.com/story/news/local/michigan/2018/08/04/candidates-historic-michigan-libertarian-primary/818356002/|title=Two candidates face off in historic Libertarian primary|work=The Detroit News|access-date=2018-09-05|language=en}} The [[Working Class Party]], [[Constitution Party (United States)|U.S. Taxpayers Party]], [[Green Party of the United States|Green Party]] and [[Natural Law Party (United States)|Natural Law Party]] chose their nominees at state party conventions.{{cite web |url=http://www.michigan.gov/documents/sos/Political_Party_Status_482649_7.pdf |title=STATE OF MICHIGAN POLITICAL PARTY STATUS |work=Michigan Department of State |author=Ruth Johnson, Secretary of State}} The race was not as close as expected, with Democrat Gretchen Whitmer being elected with 53.3% of the vote to Republican Bill Schuette's 43.8%.{{Cite web | url=https://mielections.us/election/results/2018GEN_CENR.html | title=2018 Michigan Official General Election Results - 11/06/2018 | access-date=November 8, 2018 | archive-date=February 22, 2025 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250222143212/https://mielections.us/election/results/2018GEN_CENR.html | url-status=dead }} Schuette performed best in more sparsely populated areas, while Whitmer was supported by large margins in large and medium cities, such as [[Detroit]], [[Ann Arbor]], and [[Lansing]]. Whitmer also performed well in the Detroit suburbs. Whitmer carried former Republican stronghold [[Kent County, Michigan|Kent County]] (location of her hometown [[Grand Rapids, Michigan|Grand Rapids]]), the first Democratic candidate to do so since [[James Blanchard]]'s landslide [[1986 Michigan gubernatorial election|1986 reelection]]. Democrats swept the statewide races by also holding onto the [[2018 United States Senate election in Michigan|Senate seat]] that was up for re-election, and picking up the positions of [[2018 Michigan Secretary of State election|secretary of state]] and [[2018 Michigan Attorney General election|attorney general]]. They also captured every state university trustee seat that was up for election as well as the [[Michigan Department of Education|State Board of Education]].{{Cite web | url=https://www.detroitnews.com/story/news/politics/elections/2018/11/06/michigan-education-boards-msu-um-wsu-results-winners/1825453002/ |title = Democrats roll to control of MSU, UM, WSU boards}} '''Tie:''' {{legend0|#D2B1D9|40–50%}} {{legend0|#AE8BB1|50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No votes}} | title = [[Governor of Minnesota|Governor]] | before_election = [[Mark Dayton]] | before_party = Minnesota Democratic–Farmer–Labor Party | after_election = [[Tim Walz]] | after_party = Minnesota Democratic–Farmer–Labor Party }} {{Elections in Minnesota sidebar}} The '''2018 Minnesota gubernatorial election''' took place on November 6, to elect the 41st [[governor of Minnesota]], as incumbent [[Minnesota Democratic–Farmer–Labor Party|Democratic]] (DFL) Governor [[Mark Dayton]] chose not to run for re-election for a third term. The Democratic nominee was U.S. Representative [[Tim Walz]] from [[Minnesota's 1st congressional district]], while the [[Republican Party of Minnesota|Republican Party]] nominated [[Hennepin County, Minnesota|Hennepin County]] commissioner [[Jeff Johnson (Minnesota politician)|Jeff Johnson]] for a second consecutive time. The [[Independence Party of Minnesota]] did not field a candidate for the first time since [[1994 Minnesota gubernatorial election|1994]]. Going into the election, polls showed Walz ahead; the race was characterized as lean or likely DFL. Walz went on to defeat Johnson by the largest margin for a DFL candidate since [[1986 Minnesota gubernatorial election|1986]], receiving more votes than any other gubernatorial candidate in Minnesota history. This was the first Minnesota gubernatorial election since [[1958 Minnesota gubernatorial election|1958]] in which any party won more than two consecutive elections, as well as the first time since [[1998 Minnesota gubernatorial election|1998]] that the party of the incumbent president lost. Republicans carried Traverse County for the first time since 1998, and Chippewa, Swift, Big Stone, Itasca, Kittson, Lac qui Parle, Red Lake, and Marshall counties since 1994. '''''Tie:''''' {{legend0|#d2b1d9|40–50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No votes}} | title = [[Governor of New Hampshire|Governor]] | before_election = [[Chris Sununu]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Chris Sununu]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsNH}} The '''2018 New Hampshire gubernatorial election''' took place on November 6, 2018, to elect the [[governor of New Hampshire]]. Incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] governor [[Chris Sununu]] won re-election to a second term, defeating former state senator Molly Kelly. Sununu was the first incumbent Republican to win reelection as governor since [[Steve Merrill]] was reelected in [[1994 New Hampshire gubernatorial election|1994]]. Primary elections were held on September 11, 2018. The gubernatorial election was coincident with races for the [[New Hampshire House of Representatives|state legislature]] and the [[2018 United States House of Representatives elections in New Hampshire|United States House of Representatives]]. This was one of eight Republican-held governorships up for election in a state won by [[Hillary Clinton]] in the [[2016 United States presidential election|2016 presidential election]]. ==Background== [[New Hampshire]] is one of only two states, along with [[Vermont]], where governors are elected to two-year terms. '''Tie:''' {{legend0|#ae8bb1|50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No data}} | title = [[Governor of New Mexico|Governor]] | before_election = [[Susana Martinez]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Michelle Lujan Grisham]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States)| }} {{ElectionsNM}} The '''2018 New Mexico gubernatorial election''' took place on November 6, 2018, to elect the next [[governor of New Mexico]], concurrently with the [[United States Senate election in New Mexico, 2018|election]] of [[New Mexico]]'s [[Classes of United States senators|Class I U.S. Senate seat]], as well as [[United States Senate elections, 2018|other elections]] to the [[United States Senate]] in other states, [[United States House of Representatives elections in New Mexico, 2018|elections]] to the [[United States House of Representatives]] and various [[New Mexico elections, 2018|local elections]]. This was one of eight Republican-held governorships up for election in a state carried by [[Hillary Clinton]] in the [[2016 United States presidential election|2016 presidential election]]. Incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] Governor [[Susana Martinez]] was term-limited and could not seek a third consecutive term. Following party primaries on June 5, 2018, [[United States House of Representatives|U.S. Representative]] [[Steve Pearce (politician)|Steve Pearce]] was the Republican nominee and U.S. Representative [[Michelle Lujan Grisham]] was the Democratic nominee. Lujan Grisham won the election by a substantial margin, which in fact was a complete and exact reversal of the [[2014 New Mexico gubernatorial election|2014 gubernatorial]] results. Her win also signaled a continuation of the pattern of the partisanship of the office changing every two terms, beginning with [[Gary Johnson]]'s first election in [[1994 New Mexico gubernatorial election|1994]]. Furthermore, the pattern of the partisanship changing with each officeholder was continued, a pattern first started after [[Toney Anaya]] left office in 1987. Furthermore, the margin between the candidates (57.2% to 42.8%) was the same as [[2014 New Mexico gubernatorial election|the previous election]], albeit with the parties switched. ==Background== At the presidential level, New Mexico has begun to trend into a Democratic-leaning swing state. It has gone Democratic in all but one presidential election since 1992. The only break in this trend came in 2004, when [[George W. Bush]] won it by less than a point. However, in 2008, [[Barack Obama]] won the state over [[John McCain]] by 15 points and in 2012 by 10 points over [[Mitt Romney]]. In 2016, Democrat [[Hillary Clinton]] defeated Republican [[Donald Trump]] by eight points. However, in 2010, then-District Attorney of New Mexico's Third Judicial District [[Susana Martinez]] won the election, becoming the first US Latina Governor, over Lieutenant Governor [[Diane Denish]], former running mate of two-term Democrat [[Bill Richardson]], by approximately seven points. In 2014, Martinez was re-elected over state Attorney General [[Gary King (politician)|Gary King]] by nearly 15 points. It has been described as one of the Democrats' best chances at a pickup, due to Gov. Martinez's unpopularity and because "she's leaving behind a high unemployment rate and struggling education system."Phillips, Amber, [https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/the-fix/wp/2018/01/06/the-top-10-gubernatorial-races-of-2018/ "The top 10 gubernatorial races of 2018], "The Washington Post", January 6, 2018 The 2018 primary election results show 116,311 votes for Democratic candidate [[Michelle Lujan Grisham]] and a total of 175,182 for all three Democratic candidates while Republican candidate/nominee [[Steve Pearce (politician)|Steve Pearce]] received 74,705; note that 23% of New Mexico's registered voters are third party or independents (280,000), who do not vote in the primary election. ==Republican primary== '''Tie:''' {{legend0|#d2b1d9|40–50%}} {{legend0|#AE8BB1|50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No votes}} | title = [[Governor of Nevada|Governor]] | before_election = [[Brian Sandoval]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Steve Sisolak]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsNV}} The '''2018 Nevada gubernatorial election''' took place on November 6, 2018, to elect the next [[List of governors of Nevada|governor of Nevada]]. Incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] governor [[Brian Sandoval]] was ineligible to run for re-election due to the absolute [[Term limits in the United States#Gubernatorial term limits|two-term limit]] established by the [[Constitution of Nevada|Nevada Constitution]]. [[Nevada]] is one of eight [[U.S. state]]s (or nine U.S. states and [[Territories of the United States|territory]]) that prohibits its governors or any other state and territorial executive branch officials from serving more than two terms, even if they are nonconsecutive. The candidate filing deadline was March 16, 2018 and the primary election was held on June 12, 2018.{{Cite news|url=https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_Senate_election_in_Nevada,_2018|title=United States Senate election in Nevada, 2018 - Ballotpedia|access-date=March 3, 2017|language=en-US}} The Republican nominee was [[Adam Laxalt]] and the Democratic nominee was [[Steve Sisolak]]. Sisolak won the election, becoming the first Democrat to be elected governor of Nevada since [[Bob Miller (Nevada governor)|Bob Miller]] won his second full term in [[1994 Nevada gubernatorial election|1994]], and the first non-incumbent Democrat to win since [[1982 Nevada gubernatorial election|1982]]. His overwhelming victory in [[Clark County, Nevada|Clark County]], home of [[Las Vegas]], and his narrow victory in [[Washoe County, Nevada|Washoe County]] were enough to pull him over the finish line. Sisolak became the first [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrat]] to be elected [[Governor of Nevada]] since [[Bob Miller (Nevada governor)|Bob Miller]]'s successful re-election bid in 1994. {{Election box begin|title=2018 Nevada gubernatorial election{{cite web |title=Statewide - Nevada General Election 2018 |url=https://www.nvsos.gov/silverstate2018gen/NVOther/ |website=www.nvsos.gov |publisher=Nevada Secretary of State |access-date=7 November 2020}}}} {{Election box winning candidate with party link |candidate=[[Steve Sisolak]] |party=Democratic Party (United States) |votes=480,007 |percentage=49.39% |change=+25.51% }} {{Election box candidate with party link |candidate=[[Adam Laxalt]] |party=Republican Party (United States) |votes=440,320 |percentage=45.31% |change=-25.27% }} {{Election box candidate with party link | candidate = [[None of These Candidates]] | party = |votes=18,865 |percentage=1.94% |change=-0.94% }} {{Election box candidate with party link |candidate=[[Ryan Bundy]] |party=Independent |votes=13,891 |percentage=1.43% |change=+1.43% }} {{Election box candidate with party link |candidate=Russell Best |party=Independent American Party of Nevada |votes=10,076 |percentage=1.04% |change=-1.62% }} {{Election box candidate with party link |candidate=Jared Lord |party=Libertarian Party (United States) |votes=8,640 |percentage=0.89% |change=+0.89% }} {{Election box majority |votes=39,687 |percentage=4.08% |change= }} {{Election box total |votes=971,799 |percentage=100.00% |change= }} {{Election box gain with party link |winner=Democratic Party (United States) |loser=Republican Party (United States) |swing=+50.78% }} {{Election box end}} ====By county==== While Laxalt won 15 of Nevada's county-level jurisdictions (14 counties and the independent city of Carson City), Sisolak carried the two largest, Clark (home to Las Vegas) and Washoe (home to Reno). '''Tie''': {{legend0|#d2b1d9|40–50%}} {{legend0|#ae8bb1|50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No data}} | title = Governor | before_election = [[Andrew Cuomo]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Andrew Cuomo]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }}{{Elections in New York (state) sidebar}} The '''2018 New York gubernatorial election''' occurred on November 6, 2018. Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] Governor [[Andrew Cuomo]] won a third term, defeating Republican [[Marc Molinaro]] and several minor party candidates. Cuomo defeated actress and activist [[Cynthia Nixon]] in the Democratic gubernatorial primary. Cuomo's running mate, Lt. Governor [[Kathy Hochul]], beat New York City councillor [[Jumaane Williams]] in the Democratic primary for the lieutenant governorship. Democratic candidates Cuomo and Hochul also ran on the ballot lines of the [[Independence Party of New York|Independence Party]] and the [[Women's Equality Party (New York)|Women's Equality Party]]; after Nixon and Williams withdrew from the race in October, Cuomo and Hochul received the nomination of the [[Working Families Party]] as well. Dutchess County Executive and former New York State Assemblymember [[Marc Molinaro]] was the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]], [[Conservative Party of New York|Conservative]], and [[Reform Party of New York State|Reform]] Party candidate. Molinaro's running mate was former Rye City Councilmember Julie Killian. Cuomo was sworn in for a third term as governor on January 1, 2019.{{Cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/01/01/nyregion/cuomo-ellis-island-inauguration-trump.html|title=At Inauguration, Cuomo Rallies State Against Trump|first=Shane|last=Goldmacher|date=January 1, 2019|work=The New York Times}} He would announced his resignation from the governorship on August 10, 2021, following [[Andrew Cuomo sexual harassment allegations|sexual harassment allegations]] and a [[Andrew Cuomo's response to nursing homes during the COVID-19 pandemic|nursing home scandal]] that plagued his third term.{{Cite web |date=2021-08-10 |title=Gov. Andrew Cuomo resigns over sexual harassment allegations |url=https://apnews.com/article/andrew-cuomo-resigns-17161f546bb83c32a337036ecf8d2a34 |access-date=2022-03-02 |website=AP NEWS |language=en}} He officially resigned on August 23.{{cite news |title=Cuomo's Last Day: Scandal-plagued governor to officially resign; Hochul sworn in midnight |url=https://www.fox5ny.com/news/cuomos-last-day-scandal-plagued-governor-to-officially-resign-hochul-sworn-in-after |access-date=October 3, 2026 |publisher=Fox5NY |date=August 23, 2021}} ==Background== Incumbent governor [[Andrew Cuomo]] was first elected governor in 2010 and was re-elected in 2014. As of 2018, New York gubernatorial elections operated on a split primary system; candidates for governor and lieutenant governor in each party ran in separate primary elections. In the general election, however, candidates for governor and lieutenant governor formed united tickets within each party. Also, New York allows [[electoral fusion]], in which candidates may appear on multiple ballot lines in the same election.{{cite web|url=https://auburnpub.com/blogs/eye_on_ny/eye-on-ny-why-fusion-voting-matters-in-new-york/article_9b8f542c-3ff8-11e8-91eb-0f4b9c2e2623.html|title=Eye on NY: Why fusion voting matters in New York|first=Robert |last=Harding|website=Auburn Citizen|date=April 15, 2018 }}{{cite web|url=https://www.cityandstateny.com/articles/politics/campaigns-elections/odd-ballot-lines-new-york-fusion-voting.html|title=Odd ballot lines flourish with New York's system of fusion voting|date=October 12, 2018|website=CSNY|access-date=January 23, 2019|archive-date=January 23, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190123121646/https://www.cityandstateny.com/articles/politics/campaigns-elections/odd-ballot-lines-new-york-fusion-voting.html|url-status=dead}} The results of the gubernatorial election determined [[ballot access]] and ballot order. As of 2018, a party's gubernatorial candidate had to receive 50,000 votes or more for that party to [[qualified New York political parties|obtain automatic ballot status in New York]] for the following four years.{{cite web|url=https://www.democratandchronicle.com/story/news/politics/albany/2018/11/02/election-day-2018-heres-whats-ballot-new-york/1848091002/|title=Election Day 2018: Here's what's on the ballot in New York|website=Rochester Democrat and Chronicle|last=Campbell|first=Jon|date=November 2, 2018}} The last Republican to win a gubernatorial election in New York was [[George Pataki]] in 2002.{{cite news|url=https://www.syracuse.com/politics/index.ssf/2017/08/george_pataki_wasnt_kidding_he_endorses_kid_rock_for_senate.html|title=George Pataki wasn't kidding: He endorses Kid Rock for Senate|work=Syracuse.com|last=Weiner|first=Mark|date=August 15, 2017|access-date=October 23, 2018}} ==Democratic primary== {{Main|2018 New York gubernatorial Democratic primary}} On November 15, 2016, Governor Andrew Cuomo announced his intention to seek a third term in office.{{cite web|url=http://www.nydailynews.com/news/politics/gov-cuomo-seek-reelection-run-president-article-1.2874698?cid=bitly|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161116102229/http://www.nydailynews.com/news/politics/gov-cuomo-seek-reelection-run-president-article-1.2874698?cid=bitly|url-status=dead|archive-date=November 16, 2016|title=Gov. Cuomo plans to seek reelection despite considered possible 2020 presidential candidate|last=Lovett|first=Kenneth|work=Daily News|location=New York|date=November 15, 2016|access-date=November 15, 2016}} On May 23, 2018, Cuomo secured the nomination of the Democratic Party at its state convention, winning support from more than 95% of the state delegates. No other candidates qualified for the primary ballot at the convention, as they all failed to meet the 25% delegate threshold.{{cite web|url=https://www.nydailynews.com/2018/05/24/gov-cuomo-overwhelmingly-beats-out-cynthia-nixon-for-democratic-party-nomination/|title=Gov. Cuomo overwhelmingly beats out Cynthia Nixon for Democratic Party nomination |author=Lovett, Kenneth |author2=Blain, Glenn |author3=Fisher, Janon |date=May 23, 2018|work=Daily News|archive-date=2018-05-23|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180523190832/http://www.nydailynews.com/new-york/cuomo-overwhelmingly-beats-cynthia-nixon-democratic-convention-article-1.4005644|url-access=limited|url-status=live|location=New York}} Actress and activist [[Cynthia Nixon]] sought to petition her way onto the Democratic primary ballot.{{cite news|url=https://abcnews.com/Politics/cynthia-nixon-gather-signatures-ballot-york-governor/story?id=55387202|title=Cynthia Nixon must gather signatures to get on the ballot for NY governor|date=May 23, 2018|access-date=April 10, 2018|work=ABC News|first=Chris|last=Donato}} By July 12, Nixon had obtained 65,000 signatures, which was more than four times the 15,000 signatures needed to force a primary election.{{cite news|url=https://www.thecut.com/2018/07/cynthia-nixon-got-over-65-000-signatures-for-primary-ballot.html|title=Cynthia Nixon Got 65,000+ Signatures to Appear on the Primary Ballot|date=July 13, 2018|access-date=July 24, 2018|work=The Cut|first=Gabriella|last=Paiella}} === Candidates === ====Nominee==== * [[Andrew Cuomo]], governor of New York ====Eliminated in primary==== * [[Cynthia Nixon]], actress and activist{{cite web|url=https://www.democratandchronicle.com/story/news/politics/albany/2018/03/19/cynthia-nixon-run-new-york-governor/438775002/|title=Cynthia Nixon to run for NY governor|date=March 19, 2018|access-date=March 19, 2018|work=Democrat and Chronicle|first=Jon|last=Campbell}} ====Withdrew==== * [[Randy Credico]], [[perennial candidate]] (endorsed Nixon){{Cite tweet|user=CredicoRandy|number=1001491133325807616|title=Being that I'm still dealing with the russiavape nonsense, I have decided to drop out of the gubernatorial race and endorse progressive activist @CynthiaNixon NIXON'S THE ONE! '''Tie:''' {{legend0|#d2b1d9|40–50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No votes}} | title = [[Governor of Ohio|Governor]] | before_election = [[John Kasich]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Mike DeWine]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsOH}} The '''2018 Ohio gubernatorial election''' took place on November 6, 2018, to elect the next [[governor of Ohio]], concurrently with the [[2018 United States Senate election in Ohio|election]] of [[Ohio]]'s [[Classes of United States senators|Class I U.S. Senate seat]], as well as [[2018 United States Senate elections|other elections]] to the United States Senate in other states, [[2018 United States House of Representatives elections|elections]] to the [[United States House of Representatives]], and various [[2018 United States elections#State elections|Ohio]] and [[2018 United States elections#Local elections|local elections]]. Incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] Governor [[John Kasich]] was term-limited and could not seek a third consecutive term. Republicans nominated [[Ohio Attorney General]] and former U.S. senator [[Mike DeWine]], while [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrats]] nominated former [[Consumer Financial Protection Bureau]] director and former Ohio attorney general [[Richard Cordray]]. This was the second contest between DeWine and Cordray, following the [[2010 Ohio Attorney General election|2010 attorney general election]], which DeWine won, 47.5% to 46.3%. In 2018, DeWine defeated Cordray 50.4% to 46.7%, in what was considered a minor upset. Despite Cordray's loss, he became the first Democratic gubernatorial candidate to win [[Cincinnati]]'s [[Hamilton County, Ohio|Hamilton County]] since [[Dick Celeste]] in [[1982 Ohio gubernatorial election|1982]]. Likewise, DeWine became the first Republican to win in the historically Democratic [[Monroe County, Ohio|Monroe County]] in a gubernatorial election since [[2002 Ohio gubernatorial election|2002]] as the county took a sharp turn to the right. With Democratic Senator [[Sherrod Brown]] winning re-election in the [[2018 United States Senate election in Ohio|same year]], this was the first election since [[1974 Ohio gubernatorial election|1974]] in which Ohio simultaneously voted for a gubernatorial nominee and a U.S. Senate nominee of opposite parties. '''Edmondson:''' {{legend0|#a5b0ff|40–50%}} {{legend0|#7996e2|50–60%}} {{legend0|#6674de|60–70%}} {{legend0|#584cde|70–80%}} {{legend0|#3933e5|80–90%}} {{legend0|#0d0596|≥90%}}
{{legend0|#808080|Tie}} {{legend0|#000000|No votes}} | title = [[Governor of Oklahoma|Governor]] | before_election = [[Mary Fallin]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Kevin Stitt]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) | image2 = File:Drewedmondson (cropped).jpg | nominee2 = [[Drew Edmondson]] | party2 = Democratic Party (United States) | popular_vote2 = 500,973 | percentage2 = 42.23% }} {{ElectionsOK}} The '''2018 Oklahoma gubernatorial election''' was held on November 6, 2018, to elect the next [[governor of Oklahoma]]. [[Incumbent]] [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] governor [[Mary Fallin]] was term-limited, and was prohibited by the [[Constitution of Oklahoma]] from seeking a third term. Republican Businessman [[Kevin Stitt]] was elected with 54.3% of the vote, defeating [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] nominee and former [[Attorney General of Oklahoma|Oklahoma attorney general]] [[Drew Edmondson]]. Primary elections occurred on June 26, 2018. Edmondson won the Democratic nomination outright. Stitt, however, faced a runoff election against former [[List of mayors of Oklahoma City|Oklahoma City mayor]] [[Mick Cornett]]. On August 28, 2018, Stitt won the Republican primary runoff and became the Republican nominee for the office. The [[Libertarian Party of Oklahoma|Libertarian Party]] also held a primary, which advanced to a runoff, with [[Chris Powell (politician)|Chris Powell]], a former chair of the Libertarian Party of Oklahoma, winning the nomination.{{cite web |title=2018 Election Calendar |url=https://www.ok.gov/elections/Election_Info/2018_Election_Calendar.html |access-date=May 14, 2018 |publisher=Oklahoma State Election Board}}{{cite web |title=Pre-Runoff Finance Reports: Governor's race |url=http://www.muskogeepolitico.com/2018/08/pre-runoff-finance-reports-governors.html |website=www.muskogeepolitico.com}} Stitt won the general election with 54.33% of the vote. This was the first time ever that the Libertarian Party was on the ballot in a gubernatorial election in Oklahoma,{{cite web|url=https://newsok.com/article/5589210/three-libertarians-competing-in-partys-first-oklahoma-gubernatorial-primary/|title=Three Libertarians competing in party's first Oklahoma gubernatorial primary|date=2 April 2018|website=NewsOK.com}} and the only time since [[1986 Oklahoma gubernatorial election|1986]] that a candidate from the [[First presidency of Donald Trump|incumbent president's party]] was elected Governor of Oklahoma. A member of the [[Cherokee Nation]], Stitt became the first tribally enrolled [[Native Americans in the United States|Native American]] to serve as governor of a [[U.S. state]].{{cite web|title=Only one state makes history with election of first Native governor|url=https://www.indianz.com/News/2018/11/07/only-one-state-makes-history-with-electi.asp|access-date=March 18, 2021|publisher=Indianz.com}} Despite his victory, Stitt lost four counties that voted Republican in the 2016 U.S. presidential race: Cherokee, Cleveland, Muskogee, and Oklahoma. ==Republican primary== ===Candidates=== ====Nominated==== * [[Kevin Stitt]], businessman{{cite web|url=http://www.theokie.com/2018-kevin-stitt-announces-republican-bid-for-governor/|title=2018: Kevin Stitt Announces Republican Bid For Governor|date=17 July 2017|access-date=22 May 2018}} ====Eliminated in the primary runoff==== *[[Mick Cornett]], former [[mayor of Oklahoma City]]{{cite web|url=http://kfor.com/2017/05/31/oklahoma-city-mayor-mick-cornett-announces-plan-to-run-for-governor/|title=Oklahoma City Mayor Mick Cornett announces plan to run for governor|date=2017-05-31|website=KFOR.com|access-date=2017-06-01}} ====Eliminated in the initial primary==== *Christopher Barnett, businessman{{cite web|url=http://chrisforgov.com/home|title=Christopher Barnett for Governor|website=chrisforgov.com|access-date=22 May 2018}} *[[Dan Fisher (Oklahoma)|Dan Fisher]], former state representative{{cite web|url=http://www.news9.com/story/35982458/former-rep-lawmaker-dan-fisher-to-run-for-state-governor|title=Former Rep. Stitt won 56 counties with at least 60% of the popular vote, 14 counties with at least 70%, and three counties – [[Beaver County, Oklahoma|Beaver]], [[Cimarron County, Oklahoma|Cimarron]], and [[Ellis County, Oklahoma|Ellis]] – with upwards of 80%. Stitt had the largest margin of victory in Cimarron with 73.09% more votes than Edmondson's 12.27%, the latter's lowest county performance in the election. The largest county per vote count won by Stitt was [[Tulsa County, Oklahoma|Tulsa County]], home of [[Tulsa, Oklahoma|Tulsa]]. [[Oklahoma County, Oklahoma|Oklahoma County]], of which [[Oklahoma City]] is county seat, was the only county where Stitt failed to acquire three out of every seven votes. Edmondson won [[Muskogee County, Oklahoma|Muskogee]] by a single vote, and had an 11.84% margin of victory – his only margin of victory above 10% – in Oklahoma County. Edmondson won his four counties with typically narrower margins than that of Stitt, having missed 50% of the popular vote in Muskogee. '''Tie:''' {{legend0|#d2b1d9|40–50%}} {{legend0|#ae8bb1|50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No data}} | title = [[Governor of Oregon|Governor]] | before_election = [[Kate Brown]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Kate Brown]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsOR}} The '''2018 Oregon gubernatorial election''' was held on November 6, 2018, to elect the [[governor of Oregon]] to serve a full four-year term. In the [[2016 Oregon gubernatorial special election|2016 special election]], [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] Governor [[Kate Brown]] had been elected to serve the last two years of [[John Kitzhaber]]'s term.{{cite web|url=http://koin.com/2016/11/08/oregon-governor-kate-brown-bud-pierce-election-2016/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161109164555/http://koin.com/2016/11/08/oregon-governor-kate-brown-bud-pierce-election-2016/|url-status=dead|archive-date=November 9, 2016|title=Kate Brown wins 2-year term as Oregon governor|author=KOIN 6 News Staff|publisher=KOIN 6 News|date=November 8, 2016|access-date=November 15, 2016}} The [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican Party]] nominated [[Knute Buehler]], her opponent in the [[2012 Oregon state elections#Secretary of State|2012 Oregon secretary of state election]]; the [[Independent Party of Oregon]] nominated Patrick Starnes. 2018 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election.text:

'''Tie''': {{legend0|#d2b1d9|40–50%}} {{legend0|#ae8bb1|50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No data}} | title = [[Governor of Pennsylvania|Governor]] | before_election = [[Tom Wolf]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Tom Wolf]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) | nominee2 = [[Scott Wagner]] | image2 = File:Scott Wagner - Pennsylvania Gubernatorial Candidate 2018 (cropped).jpg | party2 = Republican Party (United States) | running_mate2 = [[Jeff Bartos]] | popular_vote2 = 2,039,882 | percentage2 = 40.67% }} {{ElectionsPA}} The '''2018 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election''' took place on November 6, 2018, to elect the [[Governor of Pennsylvania|governor]] and [[lieutenant governor of Pennsylvania]], concurrently with the [[2018 United States Senate election in Pennsylvania|election]] of Pennsylvania's [[Classes of United States senators|Class I U.S. Senate seat]], [[2018 United States House of Representatives elections|elections]] to the [[United States House of Representatives]], and various [[2018 United States elections#Local elections|local elections]]. Incumbent Governor [[Tom Wolf]] won a second term by a double-digit margin, defeating [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] challenger [[Scott Wagner]] and two third-party candidates, [[Paul Glover (activist)|Paul Glover]] from the [[Green Party of the United States|Green Party]], and Ken Krawchuk from the [[Libertarian Party (United States)|Libertarian Party]].{{cite web|url=http://www.politicspa.com/pa-gov-wolf-i-am-running-for-re-election-in-2018/82004|title=Pa-Gov: Wolf: 'I am running for re-election in 2018'|publisher=PoliticsPA|date=March 7, 2017|access-date=June 15, 2017}}{{cite news |url=https://www.nbcphiladelphia.com/news/politics/Pennsylvania-Governor-Race-Tom-Wolf-Scott-Wagner-Election-Results-2018-499854871.html |publisher=[[WCAU]] |date=November 6, 2018 |title=Tom Wolf Is the Projected Winner of a Second Term as Pennsylvania Governor, Defeating Republican Challenger Scott Wagner |access-date=November 7, 2018}} The primary elections were held on May 15.{{cite web |url=http://www.ncsl.org/research/elections-and-campaigns/2018-state-primary-election-dates.aspx |title=State Primary Election Dates |website=National Conference of State Legislatures |date=January 10, 2018 |access-date=November 7, 2018 |archive-date=April 20, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180420154714/http://www.ncsl.org/research/elections-and-campaigns/2018-state-primary-election-dates.aspx |url-status=dead }} This was the only Democratic-held governorship up for election in a state that [[Donald Trump]] won in the [[2016 United States presidential election|2016 presidential election]]. Wagner won eight counties that Wolf won in 2014: [[Lawrence County, Pennsylvania|Lawrence]], [[Greene County, Pennsylvania|Greene]], [[Fayette County, Pennsylvania|Fayette]], [[Cambria County, Pennsylvania|Cambria]], [[Clinton County, Pennsylvania|Clinton]], [[Northumberland County, Pennsylvania|Northumberland]], [[Carbon County, Pennsylvania|Carbon]], and [[Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania|Schuylkill]]. Meanwhile, this was the first time since [[Bob Casey Jr.]]'s landslide state treasurer win in [[2004 Pennsylvania State Treasurer election|2004]] that [[Cumberland County, Pennsylvania|Cumberland County]] voted for the Democrat in a statewide election. ==Democratic primary== ===Governor=== ====Candidate==== =====Nominated===== * [[Tom Wolf]], incumbent governor =====Results===== {{Election box begin no change|title=Democratic primary results}}{{Election box winning candidate with party link no change|candidate=[[Tom Wolf]] (incumbent)|party=Democratic Party (United States)|votes=741,676|percentage=100.0}}{{Election box total no change|votes=741,676|percentage=100.0}}{{Election box end}} ===Lieutenant governor=== Incumbent Lieutenant Governor Mike Stack faced several controversies during his term, including mistreatment of state police officers assigned as his security detail.{{cite web |last1=Straub |first1=Mike |title=Lt. Gov. Mike Stack apologizes for how he and wife treated state troopers on security detail |url=https://www.wgal.com/article/lt-gov-mike-stack-apologizes-for-how-he-and-wife-treated-state-troopers-on-security-detail/9267886 |website=WGAL 8 |date=April 12, 2017 |access-date=2 November 2024}} As a result, he faced several challengers in the primary, including 2016 Senate candidate [[John Fetterman]]. '''Fung''': {{legend0|#ffb2b2|40–50%}} {{legend0|#e27f7f|50–60%}} {{legend0|#d75d5d|60–70%}} {{legend0|#d72f30|70–80%}} | title = [[Governor of Rhode Island|Governor]] | before_election = [[Gina Raimondo]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Gina Raimondo]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States)| }} {{ElectionsRI}} The '''2018 Rhode Island gubernatorial election''' was held on November 6, 2018, to elect the [[governor of Rhode Island]], concurrently with the [[2018 United States Senate election in Rhode Island|election]] of Rhode Island's [[Classes of United States senators|Class I U.S. Senate seat]], as well as [[2018 United States Senate elections|other elections]] to the United States Senate in other states, [[2018 United States House of Representatives elections|elections]] to the [[United States House of Representatives]], and various [[2018 United States elections#State elections|state]] and [[2018 United States elections#Local elections|local elections]]. On September 12, 2018, incumbent governor [[Gina Raimondo]] and Cranston mayor and 2014 gubernatorial nominee [[Allan Fung]] won the Democratic and Republican primaries respectively, facing each other in a rematch of the 2014 election. Raimondo defeated Fung in the general election on November 6 to win a second term as governor, improving on her plurality win in 2014 to earn a majority of the votes, and becoming the first gubernatorial candidate (incumbent or challenger) to win a majority of votes since [[Donald Carcieri]] in [[2006 Rhode Island gubernatorial election|2006]]. It was also the first time that a Democrat was re-elected as [[Governor of Rhode Island]] since [[Bruce Sundlun]] won a second term in [[1992 Rhode Island gubernatorial election|1992]], and the first
